source_title: Investigation into government's response to the collapse of Thomas Cook (NAO), corroborated by contemporaneous BBC/CNN reporting
publisher_issuer: National Audit Office (NAO), UK; corroborated by named journalism (CNN, Wikipedia summary of NAO findings)
company_context: Thomas Cook Group plc was a 178-year-old UK travel group operating tour operations, retail travel shops and an airline. It entered compulsory liquidation on 23 September 2019 after last-minute rescue financing talks failed, triggering the UK's largest peacetime repatriation.
business_type: Travel / tour operator and airline (integrated leisure travel)
geography: United Kingdom (global operations; ~600,000 customers abroad including 150,000 UK)
macro_context: Structural shift to online and dynamic-packaging travel booking, heavy legacy high-street retail estate, high debt load, the 2018 European heatwave depressing late bookings, Brexit-related uncertainty and high fuel costs.
evidence_summary: Thomas Cook carried a high debt load (reported around £1.6-1.7 billion) into 2019 while facing eroding demand for its traditional packaged-holiday and high-street model. A final rescue attempt on the evening of 22 September 2019 required additional funding that lenders/shareholders would not provide, and the group entered compulsory liquidation on 23 September 2019. Approximately 21,000 employees worldwide (including ~9,000 in the UK) lost their jobs, and about 600,000 customers (150,000 from the UK) were left abroad, triggering 'Operation Matterhorn'. Between 23 September and 7 October 2019, 746 repatriation flights from 54 airports returned 94% of passengers on their original scheduled dates.
owner_decision_context: Management sought a debt-for-equity restructuring led by major shareholder Fosun plus lenders; at the eleventh hour creditors demanded an additional ~£200m contingency that the company could not raise, forcing a binary choice between immediate liquidation and a funding gap it could not close.
action_taken: Attempted refinancing/recapitalisation through summer 2019; final overnight rescue talks on 22 September 2019 collapsed; the company entered compulsory liquidation on 23 September 2019. The UK Civil Aviation Authority and government launched Operation Matterhorn to repatriate stranded customers.
outcome_evidence: Compulsory liquidation on 23 September 2019; ~21,000 jobs lost; UK's largest peacetime repatriation (746 flights), confirming terminal insolvency driven by unsustainable debt against a declining-demand legacy model rather than a recoverable liquidity blip.
source_limitations: WebFetch of nao.org.uk returned HTTP 403; figures confirmed verbatim in WebSearch snippets attributed to the NAO report and contemporaneous CNN/Wikipedia (citing the NAO). The debt figure is cited in a £1.6-1.7bn range across sources; the precise final-rescue funding-gap figure (~£200m) is widely reported but not asserted here as exact.
directly_stated: Compulsory liquidation on 23 September 2019 after failed rescue talks the evening of 22 September
746 repatriation flights from 54 airports between 23 Sept and 7 Oct 2019
94% of passengers returned on their original scheduled date
inferred: A high fixed-cost legacy retail/airline model plus heavy debt left no buffer against demand shocks (heatwave, Brexit uncertainty)
The business was a chronic-decline solvency failure, not a one-off liquidity event
why_useful_for_opsiq: Combines structural demand erosion (legacy package-holiday model losing to online) with debt/solvency pressure, ending in disorderly liquidation. Tests whether the engine distinguishes a slow demand-generation decline compounded by leverage from a curable short-term cash crisis, and routes a failed rescue into terminal-failure classification.
